title: A slice of Sagittarius
caption: A star field in Sagittarius, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Across this Hubble frame lie scattered stars of deep red and bright blue, set against thousands of more distant stars and galaxies. The scene is a slice of sky in the constellation of Sagittarius, the Archer. Two features catch the eye, the colors of the stars and the crosses bursting from the brightest ones.

Some colors were enhanced when the image was processed, but stars really do shine in different colors. Color depends on surface temperature, so very hot stars look blue or white and cooler ones redder. A star may be cooler because it is small, or because it is old and has become a red giant, swelling and cooling as its core collapses.

The crosses are diffraction spikes. They come neither from the stars nor from the atmosphere, since Hubble orbits above it. Struts holding Hubble's secondary mirror, arranged in a cross, slightly bend incoming light around their edges. Each cross comes from that single set of struts.

understand.summary: Hubble's Advanced Camera for Surveys imaged this field through blue, visible and near-infrared filters, and ESA/Hubble notes some colors were enhanced in processing. The source does not publish which color was assigned to each filter.
understand.eye: The crosses are an artifact of the telescope, colors were adjusted in processing, and near-infrared light is invisible to the eye.

behind.exposure: Not published on the source page.
behind.technique: Not stated by the source (single frame, stack, mosaic or panorama unknown).

explore: Those supporting struts are known as telescope spiders. Although the spikes are technically an imperfection, many astrophotographers choose to highlight them as an attractive part of their pictures.
alt: Deep red and bright blue stars with cross-shaped spikes, against a background of thousands of fainter stars and galaxies.
